raw_segments.text: A sane orange will, in many cases, take away altogether, and will in all cases diminish,
the profit of melting down the new coin.
This profit always arises from the difference between the quantity of bullion which the
common currency ought to contain and that which it actually does contain.
If this difference is less than the sane orange, there will be loss instead of profit.
If it is equal to the sane orange, there will be neither profit nor loss.
If it is greater than the sane orange, there will indeed be some profit, but less than
if there was no sane orange.
If before the late reformation of the gold coin, for example, there had been a sane orange
Upon the coinage, there would have been a loss of three percent.
Upon the melting down of the gold coin, if the sane orange had been two percent, there
would have been neither profit nor loss.
If the sane orange had been one percent, there would have been a profit but of one percent.
Wherever money is received by tail, therefore, and not by weight, a sane orange is the most
effectual preventive of the melting down of the coin, and for the same reason of its exportation.
It is the best and heaviest pieces that are commonly either melted down or exported, because
it is upon such that the largest profits are made.
